blocks.html: In the plane you name a point with two numbers and measure distance with the distance formula, which is the Pythagorean theorem in disguise. Space needs one more number. A point is an ordered triple $(x, y, z)$: go $x$ units along the $x$-axis, $y$ units parallel to the $y$-axis, then $z$ units up (or down, if $z$ is negative).

The three axes are perpendicular, and their directions follow the right-hand rule: point the fingers of your right hand along the positive $x$-axis and curl them toward the positive $y$-axis; your thumb points along the positive $z$-axis. Every textbook picture and every formula later in this course (the cross product, orientations, Stokes' theorem) assumes this arrangement.

A point in space is $(x, y, z)$. The distance between $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ is
  $$d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}.$$
  The sphere with center $(a, b, c)$ and radius $r$ is every point at distance $r$ from the center: $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 + (z - c)^2 = r^2$.

Use the Pythagorean theorem twice. Walk from $P$ to $Q$ in three legs: $\Delta x$ along the $x$-direction, $\Delta y$ along the $y$-direction, then $\Delta z$ straight up. The first two legs lie in a horizontal floor and are perpendicular, so the floor diagonal has length $\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2}$. That diagonal is horizontal and the last leg is vertical, so they are perpendicular too, and
  $$d^2 = \left(\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2}\right)^2 + (\Delta z)^2 = (\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2 + (\Delta z)^2.$$

blocks.html: You already know how to add and scale vectors in the plane: work component by component. In space nothing changes except that a vector has three components, $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, v_3 \rangle$. Think of it as a displacement: $v_1$ units in the $x$-direction, $v_2$ in the $y$-direction, $v_3$ in the $z$-direction. Where you start does not matter; only the size and direction of the move do.

From $P$ to $Q$: $\overrightarrow{PQ} = Q - P$ ("end minus start"). Vectors add and scale component by component, and
  $$|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + v_3^2}, \qquad \text{unit vector in the direction of } \mathbf{v}: \ \frac{\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|}.$$
  With $\mathbf{i} = \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle$, $\mathbf{j} = \langle 0, 1, 0 \rangle$, $\mathbf{k} = \langle 0, 0, 1 \rangle$, every vector is $v_1\mathbf{i} + v_2\mathbf{j} + v_3\mathbf{k}$.

Adding two displacements means doing one move and then the other. The $x$-parts of the two moves simply add, and so do the $y$-parts and the $z$-parts, because the three directions are independent. The length formula is the 3-D distance formula applied to the move from the tail $(0, 0, 0)$ to the tip $(v_1, v_2, v_3)$. Multiplying by $c$ multiplies every component, so it multiplies the length by $|c|$; dividing by $|\mathbf{v}|$ therefore makes the length exactly ${}1$ without changing the direction.

blocks.html: In precalculus you met the dot product and projections in the plane. In space they work the same way with one more term: $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_3$. The result is a number, and that number measures how much the two vectors point the same way.

$$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_3 = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta.$$ Positive: the angle is acute. Zero: the vectors are orthogonal. Negative: obtuse. Projecting $\mathbf{u}$ onto $\mathbf{v}$: $$\operatorname{comp}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|} \ \text{(a number)}, \qquad \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\,\mathbf{v} \ \text{(a vector)}.$$

Why does a sum of products know the angle? Put $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$ into a triangle. The law of cosines says $$|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2 - 2|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta.$$ Expanding the left side with components gives $$(u_1 - v_1)^2 + (u_2 - v_2)^2 + (u_3 - v_3)^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2 - 2(u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_3).$$ Compare the two: $u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_3 = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta$.
For the projection, the shadow of $\mathbf{u}$ on the line of $\mathbf{v}$ has signed length $|\mathbf{u}|\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|}$. To turn that length into a vector, multiply by the unit vector $\frac{\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|}$: that is where $|\mathbf{v}|^2$ comes from.

blocks.html: The dot product turns two vectors into a number. In space there is a second product that turns two vectors into a vector: the cross product. It answers a question you will ask constantly in this course: which direction is perpendicular to both of these? Its formula is a 3 × 3 determinant.

$$\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \\ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \end{vmatrix} = \langle u_2v_3 - u_3v_2,\ u_3v_1 - u_1v_3,\ u_1v_2 - u_2v_1 \rangle.$$
  It is perpendicular to both $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, points by the right-hand rule, and its length $|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\sin\theta$ is the area of the parallelogram they span.

Perpendicular: dot the result with $\mathbf{u}$: $$u_1(u_2v_3 - u_3v_2) + u_2(u_3v_1 - u_1v_3) + u_3(u_1v_2 - u_2v_1) = 0,$$ because the six products cancel in pairs (it is a determinant with two equal rows). The same happens with $\mathbf{v}$.
Length: multiplying out gives Lagrange's identity $$|\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 - (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2(1 - \cos^2\theta),$$ so $|\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\sin\theta$: base $|\mathbf{u}|$ times height $|\mathbf{v}|\sin\theta$.

blocks.html: In the plane a line is $y = mx + b$, but slope does not make sense in space: there is no single "rise over run". Instead, describe a line the way you would give directions: start at a point and keep moving in one direction. You already have the tools: a point and a vector.

The line through $P_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0)$ with direction $\mathbf{v} = \langle a, b, c \rangle$ is
  $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle x_0, y_0, z_0 \rangle + t\langle a, b, c \rangle, \quad\text{that is}\quad x = x_0 + at,\ y = y_0 + bt,\ z = z_0 + ct.$$
  Through two points $P$ and $Q$: use $\mathbf{v} = \overrightarrow{PQ}$. When $a, b, c \ne 0$, solving each equation for $t$ gives the symmetric form $\frac{x - x_0}{a} = \frac{y - y_0}{b} = \frac{z - z_0}{c}$.

A point $X$ is on the line exactly when the trip from $P_0$ to $X$ is some multiple of the direction: $\overrightarrow{P_0X} = t\mathbf{v}$ for a number $t$. Rearranged, $X = P_0 + t\mathbf{v}$. Positive $t$ moves forward, negative $t$ backward, and every real $t$ gives one point. The parameter $t$ is like a clock: at $t = 0$ you are at $P_0$, at $t = 1$ you have made one full move $\mathbf{v}$.

Two lines in space can be parallel (directions are multiples), intersecting (they share a point) or skew: not parallel, yet they never meet, like a road passing over another road on a bridge. Skew lines are impossible in the plane, which is why they surprise people.

Also use different letters ($t$ and $s$) for the two parameters: the lines may pass the same point at different "times".

blocks.html: A line is fixed by a point and a direction along it. A plane is fixed by a point and a direction perpendicular to it, called a normal vector. Once you know the normal, the dot product turns "lies in the plane" into an equation, and the cross product produces a normal from two directions in the plane.

The plane through $P_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0)$ with normal $\mathbf{n} = \langle a, b, c \rangle$:
  $$a(x - x_0) + b(y - y_0) + c(z - z_0) = 0, \quad\text{or}\quad ax + by + cz = d.$$
  The coefficients of $x$, $y$, $z$ are a normal vector. Through three points $A$, $B$, $C$: $\mathbf{n} = \overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}$.

Pick any point $X = (x, y, z)$. It lies in the plane exactly when the vector $\overrightarrow{P_0X}$ runs along the plane, which means it is perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$: $\mathbf{n} \cdot \overrightarrow{P_0X} = 0$. Writing that dot product out in components is the equation above. For three points, $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ both lie in the plane, and their cross product is perpendicular to both, so it is perpendicular to the whole plane.

blocks.html: How far is a point from a plane? "Distance" always means the shortest distance, and the shortest path to a plane runs straight along its normal. So the question becomes a projection problem: how long is the part of a connecting vector that points along $\mathbf{n}$? The same idea, with a cross product, handles distances to lines.

Point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ to the plane $ax + by + cz = d$:
  $$D = \frac{|ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0 - d|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}.$$
  Point $X$ to the line through $P_0$ with direction $\mathbf{v}$: $D = \dfrac{|\overrightarrow{P_0X} \times \mathbf{v}|}{|\mathbf{v}|}$.

Choose any point $Q$ on the plane and let $\mathbf{w} = \overrightarrow{QX}$. The distance is the length of the shadow of $\mathbf{w}$ on the normal line: $D = \frac{|\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{n}|}{|\mathbf{n}|}$. Now $$\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{n} = (ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0) - (a q_1 + b q_2 + c q_3) = ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0 - d,$$ because $Q$ is on the plane. Any choice of $Q$ gives the same answer, which is why the formula needs only $d$.
For a line, the parallelogram on $\overrightarrow{P_0X}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ has area $|\overrightarrow{P_0X} \times \mathbf{v}|$ and base $|\mathbf{v}|$; its height is the distance from $X$ to the line.

The second-degree ones are called quadric surfaces, the 3-D cousins of the conics you learned to identify from their equations. The trick for picturing them: slice. Setting one variable to a constant gives a curve in that plane, called a trace, and the traces are conics you already know.

blocks.html: Take the one-sheet hyperboloid $x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 1$ and slice it at height $z = k$: the trace is $x^2 + y^2 = 1 + k^2$, a circle whose radius $\sqrt{1 + k^2}$ is never zero. Stacking these circles gives one connected surface, narrowest at $z = 0$. Now flip the signs: $z^2 - x^2 - y^2 = 1$ gives $x^2 + y^2 = k^2 - 1$, which has no points when $|k| < 1$. The surface misses the slab between $z = -1$ and $z = 1$ and splits into two pieces. Counting minus signs is just a shortcut for this slicing argument.

blocks.html: Two more situations come up often. If one variable is missing, the surface is a cylinder: $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ has the same circle as its trace at every height, so it is a round pipe around the $z$-axis, and $z = y^2$ is a parabola swept along the $x$-axis, a trough. If the equation has first-degree terms in a squared variable, complete the square to find the center: $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 4y = 0$ becomes $x^2 + (y - 2)^2 + z^2 = 4$, a sphere of radius ${}2$ centered at $(0, 2, 0)$. A good routine: complete the squares, divide so the constant is ${}1$ (if there is one), count the squared terms and their signs, and check one or two traces to be sure.

blocks.html: Rectangular coordinates are not always the easiest way to describe a shape. You already know polar coordinates for circles in the plane. Space has two natural extensions: cylindrical coordinates (polar in the floor, plus height) for things with an axis, like pipes and cans, and spherical coordinates (distance from the origin and two angles) for balls and cones.

Cylindrical $(r, \theta, z)$: $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, $z = z$, with $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$.
Spherical $(\rho, \theta, \varphi)$: $\rho$ is the distance from the origin, $\theta$ the same angle as in polar coordinates, and $\varphi$ the angle measured down from the positive $z$-axis, with $\rho \ge 0$ and ${}0 \le \varphi \le \pi$. $$x = \rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta, \quad y = \rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta, \quad z = \rho\cos\varphi, \quad \rho^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2.$$

Picture the vertical half-plane that contains the point and the $z$-axis. In it, the segment from the origin to the point has length $\rho$ and makes angle $\varphi$ with the $z$-axis. That right triangle has vertical leg $z = \rho\cos\varphi$ and horizontal leg $r = \rho\sin\varphi$, the distance from the $z$-axis. The horizontal leg points in the direction $\theta$, so polar coordinates finish the job: $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$.

blocks.html: You have already described lines in space as $\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\mathbf{v}$, and curves in the plane with parametric equations. Put the two ideas together and let each coordinate be any function of $t$: $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t) \rangle.$$ This is a vector-valued function. Think of $t$ as time and $\mathbf{r}(t)$ as the position of a moving particle; the path it traces is a space curve.

A vector function is three ordinary functions working together. Its domain is the set of $t$ where all components are defined, and limits and continuity work component by component: $$\lim_{t \to a} \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle \lim_{t \to a} f(t),\ \lim_{t \to a} g(t),\ \lim_{t \to a} h(t) \right\rangle.$$

Why can we take limits one component at a time? "$\mathbf{r}(t)$ approaches $\mathbf{L}$" means the distance $|\mathbf{r}(t) - \mathbf{L}|$ shrinks to ${}0$. Each component difference is at most that distance (a leg of a right triangle is never longer than the diagonal), and the distance is at most the sum of the three component differences. So the distance goes to ${}0$ exactly when all three component differences do.

blocks.html: A curve and its parametrization are not the same thing. $\langle \cos t, \sin t, 0 \rangle$ and $\langle \cos 2t, \sin 2t, 0 \rangle$ trace the same unit circle, the second twice as fast, and $\langle \cos t, -\sin t, 0 \rangle$ traces it the other way around. Vector functions also describe curves where two surfaces meet. The cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ and the plane $z = 1 + x$ meet in a curve: use $x = \cos t$, $y = \sin t$ to stay on the cylinder, and the plane then forces $z = 1 + \cos t$. So $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, 1 + \cos t \rangle$, ${}0 \le t \le 2\pi$: an ellipse tilted in space.

blocks.html: Calculus of vector functions needs nothing new: differentiate and integrate each component with the rules you learned for antiderivatives and derivatives. What is new is the meaning. The derivative $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ is the velocity of the moving point, and it is tangent to the curve.

$$\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle f'(t), g'(t), h'(t) \rangle, \qquad \int \mathbf{r}(t)\,dt = \left\langle \int f\,dt, \int g\,dt, \int h\,dt \right\rangle + \mathbf{C}.$$
  $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ points along the curve in the direction of motion. The tangent line at $t_0$ is $\mathbf{L}(s) = \mathbf{r}(t_0) + s\,\mathbf{r}'(t_0)$.

The derivative is a limit of difference quotients:
  $$\mathbf{r}'(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\mathbf{r}(t + h) - \mathbf{r}(t)}{h}.$$
  The vector $\mathbf{r}(t + h) - \mathbf{r}(t)$ is a secant arrow from one point of the curve to a nearby one. Dividing by $h$ rescales it, and as $h \to 0$ the arrow swings into the tangent direction. Because limits go component by component, the result is the vector of ordinary derivatives. The usual rules follow; for example $(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})' = \mathbf{u}' \cdot \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}'$, and the same pattern holds for cross products (keep the order).

blocks.html: In Calculus 2 you found the length of a curve in the plane. In space the idea is the same, and the velocity vector makes it look natural: distance traveled is speed times time, and the speed of a moving point is the length of its velocity, $|\mathbf{r}'(t)|$.

The length of the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$, $a \le t \le b$, traced once, is
  $$L = \int_a^b |\mathbf{r}'(t)|\,dt = \int_a^b \sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2 + h'(t)^2}\,dt.$$
  The arc length function $s(t) = \int_a^t |\mathbf{r}'(u)|\,du$ measures distance along the curve, and $\frac{ds}{dt} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|$.

Chop the time interval into small pieces of length $\Delta t$. Over one piece the point moves about $\mathbf{r}'(t)\,\Delta t$ (velocity times time), a straight step of length $|\mathbf{r}'(t)|\,\Delta t$. Adding the steps gives a Riemann sum $\sum |\mathbf{r}'(t_i)|\,\Delta t$, which becomes the integral as $\Delta t \to 0$. Speed, not velocity: a length is never negative and does not care about direction.

blocks.html: Two facts are worth knowing. First, the length does not depend on how the curve is parametrized, as long as it is traced once: going twice as fast doubles $|\mathbf{r}'(t)|$ but halves the time, and the substitution rule shows that the integral is unchanged. Second, the length is at least the straight-line distance between the endpoints, since $$|\mathbf{r}(b) - \mathbf{r}(a)| = \left|\int_a^b \mathbf{r}'(t)\,dt\right| \le \int_a^b |\mathbf{r}'(t)|\,dt.$$ Equality holds only for a straight segment traced without turning back.

Arc length is the parameter the curve itself prefers, which is why curvature is defined with it.

Integrating the velocity instead of the speed. $\int_a^b \mathbf{r}'(t)\,dt = \mathbf{r}(b) - \mathbf{r}(a)$ is a displacement vector, not a length. You must take the length $|\mathbf{r}'(t)|$ first, then integrate. Check: the arc length is never shorter than the straight-line distance $|\mathbf{r}(b) - \mathbf{r}(a)|$.

blocks.html: A road can be gently curved or tightly bent. Curvature puts a number on that: how fast the direction of travel turns per unit of distance. It builds on the arc length you just met, because "per unit of distance" means per unit of $s$, not per unit of time.

Unit tangent $\mathbf{T}(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf{r}'(t)}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|}$. Curvature
  $$\kappa = \left|\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}\right| = \frac{|\mathbf{T}'(t)|}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|} = \frac{|\mathbf{r}'(t) \times \mathbf{r}''(t)|}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|^3}.$$
  For a graph $y = f(x)$: $\kappa = \dfrac{|f''(x)|}{\left(1 + f'(x)^2\right)^{3/2}}$. The unit normal $\mathbf{N} = \dfrac{\mathbf{T}'}{|\mathbf{T}'|}$ points toward the inside of the bend.

$\mathbf{T}$ only carries direction (length 1), so its rate of change measures turning. But $\mathbf{T}'(t)$ is a rate per unit time: drive the same road twice as fast and it doubles. Dividing by the speed $\frac{ds}{dt} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|$ converts it to a rate per unit distance, a property of the road alone.
Check on a circle of radius $R$: $\mathbf{r} = \langle R\cos t, R\sin t \rangle$ has speed $R$ and $\mathbf{T} = \langle -\sin t, \cos t \rangle$, so $|\mathbf{T}'| = 1$ and $\kappa = \frac{1}{R}$. Small circles bend sharply. Also, since $\mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{T} = 1$, differentiating gives ${}2\mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{T}' = 0$: $\mathbf{T}'$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{T}$, which is why $\mathbf{N}$ is a normal.

blocks.html: Back to physics. In one dimension velocity and acceleration were numbers along a line. In space they are vectors: $\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{r}'(t)$, speed $|\mathbf{v}(t)|$, and $\mathbf{a}(t) = \mathbf{r}''(t)$. The new question is what acceleration does: part of it speeds you up or slows you down, and part of it turns you.

Acceleration splits into a tangential part and a normal part:
  $$\mathbf{a} = a_T\,\mathbf{T} + a_N\,\mathbf{N}, \qquad a_T = \frac{d|\mathbf{v}|}{dt} = \frac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{v}|}, \qquad a_N = \kappa|\mathbf{v}|^2 = \frac{|\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{a}|}{|\mathbf{v}|}.$$
  $a_T$ changes the speed; $a_N \ge 0$ changes the direction.

Write the velocity as speed times direction: $\mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{v}|\,\mathbf{T}$. Differentiate with the product rule: $$\mathbf{a} = \frac{d|\mathbf{v}|}{dt}\,\mathbf{T} + |\mathbf{v}|\,\mathbf{T}'.$$ From the curvature lesson, $\mathbf{T}' = |\mathbf{T}'|\,\mathbf{N} = \kappa|\mathbf{v}|\,\mathbf{N}$. So $\mathbf{a} = \frac{d|\mathbf{v}|}{dt}\mathbf{T} + \kappa|\mathbf{v}|^2\mathbf{N}$. That is why a car taking a curve twice as fast needs four times the sideways force.

blocks.name: param3d
blocks.cap: A projectile path. $\mathbf{T}$ follows the motion and $\mathbf{N}$ points toward the inside of the curve, downward here. Gravity pulls straight down, so it has a tangential part (slowing the rise) and a normal part (bending the path).

steps: $a_T = \frac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{v}|} = \frac{4 + 0 - 1}{3} = 1$: the speed grows by 1 unit per second per second.

blocks.title: A projectile
blocks.q: A ball leaves the ground with $\mathbf{v}(0) = \langle 20, 10, 64 \rangle$ ft/s; gravity gives $\mathbf{a} = \langle 0, 0, -32 \rangle$. Where does it land, and how high does it go?
steps: Integrate: $\mathbf{v}(t) = \langle 20, 10, 64 - 32t \rangle$ and, starting at the origin, $\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 20t, 10t, 64t - 16t^2 \rangle$.
Top: vertical velocity ${}64 - 32t = 0$ at $t = 2$, height ${}128 - 64 = 64$ ft.

blocks.html: Thinking constant speed means no acceleration. A car going around a circle at a steady 30 mph has $a_T = 0$, but its direction keeps changing, so $a_N = \kappa|\mathbf{v}|^2 \ne 0$. Acceleration is the change in the velocity vector. Also: $a_N$ is never negative (it is a length along $\mathbf{N}$), while a negative $a_T$ simply means slowing down. A useful check is $a_T^2 + a_N^2 = |\mathbf{a}|^2$.

sources.name: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3, 3.4 Motion in Space

blocks.html: So far a function took one number and returned one number. Many quantities depend on two: the height of land depends on east-west and north-south position; the temperature on a metal plate depends on $x$ and $y$. A function of two variables $z = f(x, y)$ assigns one number to each point of a region of the plane, its domain. Its graph is a surface in space, like the quadric surfaces you have met.

Surfaces are hard to draw by hand, so we borrow an idea from hiking maps. Slice the graph with horizontal planes $z = k$ and drop each slice onto the $xy$-plane. Each curve $f(x, y) = k$ is a level curve (contour), and a family of them is a contour map.

The level curve $f(x, y) = k$ collects every point where $f$ has the value $k$. If the levels are equally spaced in height, then level curves that are close together mean the surface is steep there, and curves far apart mean it is gentle.

Neighboring contours differ by the same height step $\Delta z$. If you must walk a horizontal distance $d$ to get from one to the next, the average slope along that walk is $\frac{\Delta z}{d}$. Same rise, shorter run: a bigger slope. This is the same rise-over-run idea as the slope of a line, measured on the map.

blocks.name: surface

blocks.title: Domain and range
blocks.q: Find the domain and range of $f(x, y) = \sqrt{9 - x^2 - y^2}$, and describe its graph.
steps: The square root needs ${}9 - x^2 - y^2 \ge 0$, that is $x^2 + y^2 \le 9$: the closed disk of radius 3.
The quantity under the root runs from ${}0$ (on the edge) to ${}9$ (at the center), so $f$ runs from ${}0$ to ${}3$.
Squaring $z = \sqrt{9 - x^2 - y^2}$ gives $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$ with $z \ge 0$: the upper half of a sphere.

Same height step, shorter gaps: the bowl is steeper farther from the origin.

sources.name: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3, 4.1 Functions of Several Variables

blocks.html: A function of three variables, $w = f(x, y, z)$, gives a number at every point of space: the temperature in a room, the density inside a planet, the pressure in the air. Its graph would need four dimensions, so we use the idea that worked for contour maps one dimension up.

A level surface of $f$ is the set $f(x, y, z) = k$. Through each point of the domain passes exactly one level surface: the one with $k$ equal to the value of $f$ there. Together, the level surfaces fill space in layers, like the skins of an onion.

A point has only one value of $f$, so it cannot lie on two level surfaces with different $k$. That is why level surfaces never cross each other, just as contour lines on a map never cross. Picturing the layers tells you how $f$ changes: moving within one layer keeps $f$ constant, and moving across layers changes it.

blocks.html: Level surfaces have physical names: in a temperature field they are isothermal surfaces, and for an electric potential they are equipotential surfaces. How closely the layers are packed shows how fast $f$ changes: tightly packed layers mean a steep change. Every graph is also a level surface: $z = g(x, y)$ is the level surface $F = 0$ of $F(x, y, z) = z - g(x, y)$. This point of view pays off with gradients and normal vectors, where the gradient of $f$ turns out to be perpendicular to the level surface through each point.

$k = -1$: $z^2 - x^2 - y^2 = 1$, a hyperboloid of two sheets.

steps: The level surface is the plane ${}2x - y + 3z = 4$.

blocks.html: Treating a level surface as the graph of $f$. The surface $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$ is not "the graph of $f = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$"; it is the set where that function equals ${}9$. The function's values are not drawn as heights at all; they label the layers. Check: every point on one level surface gives the same value of $f$.

blocks.html: In one variable, $x$ can approach $a$ from only two sides, and the precise definition of a limit asks for closeness on both. In the plane, a point can approach $(a, b)$ along infinitely many paths: straight lines from every direction, parabolas, spirals. A limit exists only if the function settles on one value no matter how you approach.

$\displaystyle\lim_{(x, y) \to (a, b)} f(x, y) = L$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $|f(x, y) - L| < \varepsilon$ whenever ${}0 < \sqrt{(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2} < \delta$.
To show a limit does not exist: find two paths that give different values. To show it exists: squeeze it, often with polar coordinates $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, where $(x, y) \to (0, 0)$ means $r \to 0$ for every $\theta$.

The definition talks about every point in a small disk around $(a, b)$, not about any particular path. If the limit is $L$, then any path into $(a, b)$ eventually stays inside the disk, so every path gives $L$. Turned around: two paths with different values make a limit impossible. But checking many paths can never prove a limit exists, because there are always paths you have not tried. A proof has to control all points at once, and a bound like $|f(x, y) - L| \le C r$ does exactly that.

Different values on two paths, so the limit does not exist.

steps: As $(x, y) \to (0, 0)$, $r \to 0$, so $f \to 0$ along every path at once.

blocks.html: Polynomials are continuous everywhere, and so are rational functions wherever the denominator is not zero; sums, products and compositions of continuous functions are continuous. For those, the limit is just the value: substitute.

Checking only straight lines. In the second example every line gives ${}0$, yet the limit does not exist: the parabola $y = x^2$ gives $\frac{1}{2}$. Agreement along lines is evidence, not proof. Either find a path that disagrees (try $y = x^2$ or $x = y^2$ when the powers in the denominator differ) or prove the limit with a bound that holds for all points near the origin.

sources.name: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3, 4.2 Limits and Continuity

blocks.html: How fast does $f(x, y)$ change? It depends on which way you move. The simplest choice is to move in the $x$-direction only, keeping $y$ fixed, or in the $y$-direction only. Each choice turns $f$ into a function of one variable, and you already know how to differentiate those, including with the chain rule.

$$f_x(a, b) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h, b) - f(a, b)}{h}, \qquad f_y(a, b) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a, b + h) - f(a, b)}{h}.$$
  To compute $f_x$, treat $y$ as a constant and differentiate with respect to $x$; for $f_y$, treat $x$ as a constant. Other notations: $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$, $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$.

Fix $y = b$. Then $g(x) = f(x, b)$ is an ordinary function, and its graph is the curve where the vertical plane $y = b$ cuts the surface (the trace). The definition of $f_x(a, b)$ is exactly the definition of $g'(a)$. So $f_x(a, b)$ is the slope of that trace, rise in $z$ per unit step in $x$. Every rule from one-variable calculus applies, because during the computation $y$ really is just a number.

blocks.name: calc3-tangent
blocks.cap: The orange curve is the trace in the plane $y = b$; its tangent line has slope $f_x$. The purple trace lies in $x = a$, with slope $f_y$. Move the point with the sliders and watch both slopes in the readout.

blocks.title: A polynomial
blocks.q: Find $f_x$ and $f_y$ for $f(x, y) = x^3y^2 + 4xy - 5y$.
steps: $f_x$: $y$ is a constant. $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^3y^2) = 3x^2y^2$, $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(4xy) = 4y$, and $-5y$ has no $x$, so its derivative is ${}0$.
$f_y$: $x$ is a constant. $\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^3y^2) = 2x^3y$, $\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(4xy) = 4x$, $\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(-5y) = -5$.

blocks.title: The chain rule inside
blocks.q: Find $f_x$ and $f_y$ for $f(x, y) = e^{xy} + x\sin y$.
steps: $f_x$: the derivative of $e^{xy}$ with respect to $x$ is $e^{xy} \cdot y$ (the inside $xy$ has $x$-derivative $y$). $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x\sin y) = \sin y$.

blocks.title: Slopes on a surface
blocks.q: For $f(x, y) = 4 - x^2 - 2y^2$, find the slopes of the surface at $(1, 1)$ in the $x$- and $y$-directions.
steps: $f_x = -2x$, so $f_x(1, 1) = -2$: stepping east, the surface drops 2 units per unit.
$f_y = -4y$, so $f_y(1, 1) = -4$: stepping north, it drops twice as fast.

blocks.html: Three variables work the same way: for $f(x, y, z) = xy^2z^3$, $f_z = 3xy^2z^2$, holding both $x$ and $y$ constant.

Differentiating the other variable too. When computing $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2y^3)$, the factor $y^3$ is a constant multiplier, so the answer is ${}2xy^3$, not ${}2x \cdot 3y^2$. And a term with no $x$ at all, like $-5y$, is a constant whose $x$-derivative is ${}0$. Check: replace $y$ by a number like ${}2$ in the original, differentiate the one-variable function, and compare.

sources.name: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3, 4.3 Partial Derivatives

blocks.html: The partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ are themselves functions of $x$ and $y$, so you can differentiate them again. That gives four second partials: $f_{xx}$, $f_{yy}$ and two mixed partials, $f_{xy}$ and $f_{yx}$.

$f_{xy} = (f_x)_y$: differentiate in $x$ first, then $y$. In Leibniz notation this is $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}$ (read right to left). Clairaut's theorem: if $f_{xy}$ and $f_{yx}$ are continuous near a point, they are equal there.

Both mixed partials come from the same "double difference" $$\Delta = f(a + h, b + k) - f(a + h, b) - f(a, b + k) + f(a, b).$$ Group it as $$[f(a + h, b + k) - f(a, b + k)] - [f(a + h, b) - f(a, b)]$$ and it measures how an $x$-change depends on $y$; group it the other way and it measures how a $y$-change depends on $x$. Dividing by $hk$ and letting $h, k \to 0$ in one order gives $f_{xy}$, in the other order $f_{yx}$. When the second partials are continuous, the order of the limits does not matter, so the two agree.
Meaning: $f_{xx}$ is the concavity of the trace in the $x$-direction; $f_{xy}$ measures twist: how the $x$-slope changes as you step in $y$.

blocks.name: surface
blocks.cap: For the saddle $z = x^2 - y^2$, $f_{xx} = 2 > 0$: traces in the $x$-direction bend up (the red slice). Switch to slices $x = c$: they bend down, matching $f_{yy} = -2$.

blocks.title: All four second partials
blocks.q: Find the second partials of $f(x, y) = x^3y^2 - 4xy^3$.

blocks.title: With an exponential
blocks.q: Find $f_{xx}$, $f_{yy}$ and $f_{xy}$ for $f(x, y) = e^{2x}\sin y$.
steps: $f_y = e^{2x}\cos y$, so $f_{yy} = -e^{2x}\sin y$ (and $f_{yx} = 2e^{2x}\cos y$ again).

blocks.title: A consistency test
blocks.q: Could $f_x = 2xy + y$ and $f_y = x^2 + 3y^2$ belong to one smooth function?
steps: They differ, so no smooth $f$ has these partials.

blocks.html: Reading the order backwards. $f_{xy}$ means $x$ first, then $y$; $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}$ means the same thing (the variable nearest $f$ goes first). For smooth functions the order does not change the answer, which makes this a perfect check on your algebra: compute both mixed partials, and if they differ, look for a mistake.

sources.name: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3, 4.3 Partial Derivatives

blocks.html: In one variable, the tangent line is the best straight-line approximation of a curve near a point. For a smooth surface, the best flat approximation is a tangent plane. You know how to write a plane from a point and a normal vector, and the two partial derivatives give you everything you need.

The tangent plane to $z = f(x, y)$ at $(a, b, f(a, b))$ is $$z = f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)(x - a) + f_y(a, b)(y - b).$$ Its right side is the linearization $L(x, y)$, and $f(x, y) \approx L(x, y)$ near $(a, b)$. A normal vector is $\langle f_x(a, b), f_y(a, b), -1 \rangle$.

The plane must contain the tangent lines of both traces. Along the $x$-trace, a step of ${}1$ in $x$ raises $z$ by $f_x$, so that tangent line has direction $\langle 1, 0, f_x \rangle$; the $y$-trace gives $\langle 0, 1, f_y \rangle$. Their cross product is a normal: $$\langle 1, 0, f_x \rangle \times \langle 0, 1, f_y \rangle = \langle -f_x, -f_y, 1 \rangle.$$ The plane through $(a, b, z_0)$ with this normal is $$-f_x(x - a) - f_y(y - b) + (z - z_0) = 0,$$ which rearranges to the formula above.

blocks.cap: The red patch is the tangent plane. Both tangent lines (orange and purple) lie in it. Move the point: near it, the plane and the surface are nearly the same, which is why $L(x, y)$ approximates $f$ well for small steps.

blocks.q: Find the tangent plane to $z = x^2 + 3xy - y^2$ at $(1, 2)$.

steps: Let $f(x, y) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ near the friendly point $(3, 4)$, where $f = 5$.

blocks.q: Find the linearization of $f(x, y) = e^{x - y}$ at $(1, 1)$.

blocks.html: Leaving $x$ and $y$ inside the slopes. The coefficients in the tangent plane are the numbers $f_x(a, b)$ and $f_y(a, b)$. If your "plane" contains $x^2$ or $xy$, you forgot to evaluate them at the point. Check: a plane is linear in $x$, $y$, $z$, and it must pass through the point of tangency.

sources.name: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3, 4.4 Tangent Planes and Linear Approximations

blocks.html: Measurements are never exact. If you measure a can's radius and height, each a little off, how far off is the volume you compute? The tangent plane answers this: for small changes, the surface is nearly flat, and the change along the plane is easy to compute.

The differential of $z = f(x, y)$ is $$dz = f_x\,dx + f_y\,dy.$$ For small changes $dx$, $dy$, the true change $\Delta z$ is approximately $dz$. To bound the error in a computed quantity, use the largest possible measurement errors and add the sizes of the terms: $|dz| \le |f_x||dx| + |f_y||dy|$.

Moving from $(a, b)$ to $(a + dx, b + dy)$ along the tangent plane changes the height by $f_x\,dx + f_y\,dy$: the $x$-slope times the $x$-step plus the $y$-slope times the $y$-step. Since the plane hugs the surface near the point, the real change differs from $dz$ only by a much smaller amount (roughly the square of the step). Dividing by $z$ gives relative error: for $Q = kx^ay^b$, $\frac{dQ}{Q} = a\frac{dx}{x} + b\frac{dy}{y}$, so percent errors add, each multiplied by its power.

blocks.name: calc3-tangent
blocks.cap: $z = xy$ (the area of an $x$ by $y$ rectangle). The red tangent plane is the "differential" world: for small steps, its rise $dz = y\,dx + x\,dy$ matches the surface's rise.

blocks.title: A differential
blocks.q: For $z = x^2y$, compare $dz$ with $\Delta z$ at $(2, 3)$ when $dx = 0.1$ and $dy = -0.05$.
steps: Exact: $$(2.1)^2(2.95) - 12 = 13.0095 - 12 = 1.0095.$$ The differential is off by less than ${}0.01$.

blocks.title: Error in a volume
blocks.q: A can measures $r = 5$ cm and $h = 10$ cm, each to within ${}0.1$ cm and ${}0.2$ cm. Estimate the largest error in $V = \pi r^2h$.
steps: Relative: $V = 250\pi$, so the error is about $\frac{15\pi}{250\pi} = 6\%$, which is ${}2(2\%) + 2\%$, as the power rule predicts.

blocks.title: Percent errors
blocks.q: The period of a pendulum is computed from $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$. If $L$ is off by at most ${}1\%$ and $g$ by at most ${}0.5\%$, how far off can $T$ be?

blocks.html: Letting errors cancel. In $dV = V_r\,dr + V_h\,dh$, the measurement errors could have either sign. To find the largest possible error, both must push the same way, so add the absolute values. Using the signs as given is right only when you know the actual changes.

sources.name: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3, 4.4 Tangent Planes and Linear Approximations

blocks.html: Suppose the temperature at a point is $T(x, y)$ and you walk along a path $x(t)$, $y(t)$. How fast does the temperature you feel change? It changes because $x$ changes and because $y$ changes, and both effects add. This is the partial derivative version of the one-variable chain rule.

If $z = f(x, y)$ with $x = x(t)$ and $y = y(t)$:
  $$\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}.$$
  If $x$ and $y$ depend on $s$ and $t$, then $\frac{\partial z}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}$. In general: multiply along each path of a tree diagram and add over all paths.

By the linear approximation, a small change gives $\Delta z \approx f_x\,\Delta x + f_y\,\Delta y$. Divide by $\Delta t$: $$\frac{\Delta z}{\Delta t} \approx f_x\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} + f_y\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t}.$$ As $\Delta t \to 0$ the approximation becomes exact and each quotient becomes a derivative. Each term is one route by which $t$ influences $z$.

A tree diagram keeps track of the routes. Put $z$ at the top, the intermediate variables in the middle, and the independent variables at the bottom. Label each branch with its derivative. For $\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}$, follow every path from $z$ down to $s$, multiply the labels along it, and add.

blocks.title: Along a path
blocks.q: Let $z = x^2y$ with $x = \cos t$, $y = \sin t$. Find $\frac{dz}{dt}$, and its value at $t = 0$.
steps: $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 2xy$, $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = x^2$, $\frac{dx}{dt} = -\sin t$, $\frac{dy}{dt} = \cos t$.
$$\frac{dz}{dt} = 2xy(-\sin t) + x^2\cos t = -2\cos t\sin^2 t + \cos^3 t.$$
At $t = 0$: ${}0 + 1 = 1$. Check: $z(t) = \cos^2 t\sin t$, whose derivative at ${}0$ is also ${}1$.
blocks.a: $\frac{dz}{dt} = \cos^3 t - 2\cos t\sin^2 t$; it equals ${}1$ at $t = 0$

blocks.title: Two independent variables
blocks.q: Let $z = x^2 + xy$ with $x = s + t$ and $y = st$. Find $\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}$ at $(s, t) = (1, 2)$.
steps: Paths to $s$: $z \to x \to s$ and $z \to y \to s$.
$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 2x + y$, $\frac{\partial x}{\partial s} = 1$, $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = x$, $\frac{\partial y}{\partial s} = t$.

blocks.title: Three intermediate variables
blocks.q: If $w = f(x, y, z)$ and $x$, $y$, $z$ are functions of $t$, write $\frac{dw}{dt}$.
steps: Three routes lead from $w$ to $t$, one through each intermediate variable.
$\frac{dw}{dt} = \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{dz}{dt}$, which is $\nabla w \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$.

blocks.html: Leaving out a path. If $y$ also depends on $t$ but you write only $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt}$, you have counted the change through $x$ and ignored the change through $y$. Draw the tree and count the paths from the top variable to the bottom one: that is the number of terms. Check with a direct substitution when the functions are simple.

sources.name: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3, 4.5 The Chain Rule

blocks.html: In Calculus 1 you found slopes of curves like $x^3 + y^3 = 6xy$ by implicit differentiation. The multivariable chain rule turns that process into a one-line formula, and it extends to surfaces given implicitly.

If $F(x, y) = 0$ defines $y$ as a function of $x$ (and $F_y \ne 0$):
  $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{F_x}{F_y}.$$
  If $F(x, y, z) = 0$ defines $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$ (and $F_z \ne 0$): $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -\frac{F_y}{F_z}$.

Along the curve, $F(x, y(x))$ stays equal to ${}0$, so its derivative with respect to $x$ is ${}0$. By the chain rule with the two paths $F \to x$ and $F \to y \to x$:
  $$F_x \cdot 1 + F_y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0.$$
  Solve for $\frac{dy}{dx}$: the minus sign comes from moving $F_x$ to the other side. For surfaces, hold $y$ fixed and do the same with $z(x, y)$: $F_x + F_z\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 0$.

blocks.cap: The bold curve through $(3, 3)$ is $x^3 + y^3 - 6xy = 0$, the folium. The blue direction $u$ at ${}135^\circ$ runs along the curve there: its slope is $-1 = -\frac{F_x}{F_y}$, and the directional derivative is ${}0$.

blocks.q: Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ for $x^3 + y^3 = 6xy$ at $(3, 3)$.

blocks.q: Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ for $x^2 + xy + y^2 = 7$.
steps: $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$, the same as differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ and solving.

blocks.title: A surface
blocks.q: The sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$ defines $z$ near $(1, 2, 2)$. Find $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ there.
steps: Check: on the top half $z = \sqrt{9 - x^2 - y^2}$, and $z_x = \frac{-x}{\sqrt{9 - x^2 - y^2}} = -\frac{1}{2}$.

blocks.html: Forgetting the minus sign. It is easy to write $\frac{F_x}{F_y}$. Test on a circle $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ at $(3, 4)$: the slope must be negative there (the top right of the circle slopes down), and $-\frac{F_x}{F_y} = -\frac{6}{8} = -\frac{3}{4}$ is. Also keep the right variable in the denominator: $F_z$ for $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$, $F_y$ for $\frac{dy}{dx}$.

blocks.html: The partial derivatives measure change heading east ($f_x$) or north ($f_y$). A hiker can head any way. The directional derivative $D_{\mathbf{u}}f$ measures the rate of change of $f$ per unit of distance in the direction of a unit vector $\mathbf{u}$, using the dot product.

For a unit vector $\mathbf{u} = \langle u_1, u_2 \rangle$:
  $$D_{\mathbf{u}}f(a, b) = f_x(a, b)\,u_1 + f_y(a, b)\,u_2 = \nabla f(a, b) \cdot \mathbf{u},$$
  where $\nabla f = \langle f_x, f_y \rangle$. If a direction is given by a vector $\mathbf{v}$ that is not unit length, use $\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|}$. For an angle $\theta$, $\mathbf{u} = \langle \cos\theta, \sin\theta \rangle$.

Walk from $(a, b)$ in direction $\mathbf{u}$: after distance $s$ you are at $x = a + su_1$, $y = b + su_2$. The chain rule gives $$\frac{d}{ds}f(a + su_1, b + su_2) = f_x\frac{dx}{ds} + f_y\frac{dy}{ds} = f_x u_1 + f_y u_2.$$ This is a rate per unit of distance because $s$ is distance, and $s$ is distance only when $|\mathbf{u}| = 1$. With a longer vector, the "distance" would really be a multiple of $s$ and the rate would be scaled by that multiple.

The direction is the same, but the rate per unit distance is not. Check: in the directions $\langle 1, 0 \rangle$ and $\langle 0, 1 \rangle$ your formula must give $f_x$ and $f_y$.

blocks.html: The vector $\nabla f = \langle f_x, f_y \rangle$ that appeared in directional derivatives deserves its own name: the gradient ("del $f$"). It packs every directional derivative into one arrow, and that arrow has a clear meaning.

At each point, $
abla f$ points in the direction in which $f$ increases fastest, and its length $|
abla f|$ is that fastest rate. $f$ decreases fastest in the direction $-
abla f$, and does not change at all in the directions perpendicular to $
abla f$.

For a unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ at angle $	heta$ to the gradient,
  $$D_{\mathbf{u}}f = 
abla f \cdot \mathbf{u} = |
abla f|\,|\mathbf{u}|\cos	heta = |
abla f|\cos	heta.$$
  Since $\cos	heta$ is between $-1$ and ${}1$, the rate is largest ($|
abla f|$) at $	heta = 0$, smallest ($-|
abla f|$) at $	heta = \pi$, and zero at $	heta = \pm rac{\pi}{2}$. Nothing about the formula for $f$ entered: this is true for every differentiable function.

steps: Perpendicular to $\nabla f = \langle 2, 4 \rangle$: swap the components and change one sign, $\pm\langle -4, 2 \rangle$.
As unit vectors: $\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\langle -2, 1 \rangle$. These run along the level curve through $(1, 1)$.

blocks.html: Drawing the gradient on the surface. $\nabla f$ has two components, so it lives in the $xy$-plane: it tells the hiker which way to step on the map. It is not tangent to the surface $z = f(x, y)$ and does not point up the hill in 3-D. (The steepest path on the surface rises above it, in the direction $\langle f_x, f_y, |\nabla f|^2 \rangle$.) Check: your gradient arrow should cross the level curves of a contour map at right angles.

sources.name: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3, 4.6 Directional Derivatives and the Gradient

blocks.html: The gradient points in the direction of fastest increase, and the rate of change is zero along a level curve. Put those together: the gradient must be perpendicular to the level curves. In three variables the same reasoning makes $\nabla F$ perpendicular to level surfaces, and that gives tangent planes to surfaces that are not graphs.

$
abla F(P)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $F(x, y, z) = k$ at $P$. The tangent plane there is
  $$F_x(P)(x - x_0) + F_y(P)(y - y_0) + F_z(P)(z - z_0) = 0,$$
  and the normal line is $\mathbf{r}(t) = P + t\,
abla F(P)$. In two variables, $
abla f$ is perpendicular to the level curve through the point.

Take any curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ lying in the level surface and passing through $P$. Along it, $F(\mathbf{r}(t)) = k$ is constant, so by the chain rule $$\frac{d}{dt}F(\mathbf{r}(t)) = \nabla F \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) = 0.$$ The gradient is perpendicular to the velocity of every curve in the surface through $P$, so it is perpendicular to the whole tangent plane. For a graph $z = f(x, y)$, use $F = f(x, y) - z$: $\nabla F = \langle f_x, f_y, -1 \rangle$, the same normal as in tangent planes.

For the surface $z = f(x, y)$, the vector $\nabla f = \langle f_x, f_y \rangle$ is perpendicular to level curves in the plane, not to the surface. blocks.html: In one variable, local extremes happen where $f'(x) = 0$, and the second derivative test tells a valley from a peak. Surfaces have one new kind of flat spot: a saddle point, like the middle of a horse's saddle or a mountain pass, which is a low point in one direction and a high point in another.

If $f$ has a local maximum or minimum at an interior point $(a, b)$ where it is differentiable, then $\nabla f(a, b) = \mathbf{0}$: a critical point. To classify it, compute $$D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - (f_{xy})^2 \text{ at } (a, b).$$ $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} > 0$: local minimum. $D > 0$ and $f_{xx} < 0$: local maximum. $D < 0$: saddle point. $D = 0$: the test says nothing.

Why $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$: if $f$ is largest at $(a, b)$ among nearby points, then in particular the trace $f(x, b)$ is largest at $x = a$, so $f_x(a, b) = 0$; likewise $f_y(a, b) = 0$.
Why $D$: near a critical point, the second-order approximation is $f \approx f(a, b) + \frac{1}{2}(Ah^2 + 2Bhk + Ck^2)$ with $A = f_{xx}$, $B = f_{xy}$, $C = f_{yy}$ and steps $h$, $k$. Completing the square (for $A \ne 0$): $$Ah^2 + 2Bhk + Ck^2 = A\left(h + \frac{B}{A}k\right)^2 + \frac{AC - B^2}{A}k^2.$$ If $AC - B^2 > 0$, both terms have the sign of $A$ for every nonzero step: a bowl ($A > 0$) or a dome ($A < 0$). If $AC - B^2 < 0$, the two terms have opposite signs, so some steps go up and others go down: a saddle.

blocks.name: surface
blocks.cap: $f(x, y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2$ has a local minimum at $(1, 0)$ and a saddle at $(-1, 0)$. The slice $y = 0$ shows the trace $x^3 - 3x$: a valley at $x = 1$ and a peak at $x = -1$. But in the $y$-direction both points sit at the bottom of $y^2$; at $(-1, 0)$ that makes a saddle.

blocks.html: Critical points also include points where a partial derivative does not exist, such as the tip of the cone $f(x, y) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$, which is a minimum even though $\nabla f$ is undefined there. And not every critical point is an extreme value: at a saddle the tangent plane is horizontal, but the surface rises above it in some directions and falls below it in others. In applications, critical points mark equilibria, such as the lowest energy state of a physical system, and the test decides whether such an equilibrium is stable (a minimum of the energy) or not.

blocks.title: A quadratic
blocks.q: Find and classify the critical points of $f(x, y) = x^2 + xy + y^2 - 3x$.
steps: $f_x = 2x + y - 3 = 0$ and $f_y = x + 2y = 0$. From the second, $x = -2y$; then $-4y + y = 3$, so $y = -1$, $x = 2$.

steps: At $(1, 0)$: $D = 12 > 0$, $f_{xx} = 6 > 0$: local minimum. At $(-1, 0)$: $D = -12 < 0$: saddle point.

blocks.html: Misreading $D$. When $D < 0$ the point is a saddle, whatever the sign of $f_{xx}$; $f_{xx}$ only matters when $D > 0$. When $D = 0$, do not conclude anything: $x^4 + y^4$, $-x^4 - y^4$ and $x^4 - y^4$ all have $D = 0$ at the origin, and they have a minimum, a maximum and a saddle there. Look at the function itself in that case.

blocks.html: A critical point finds local highs and lows inside a region, but the highest point of a whole region is often on its edge. Think of a sloping field: its highest point is at a fence, where the gradient is not zero at all. As in Calculus 1, where you checked endpoints, the boundary must be checked too.
A continuous function on a closed, bounded region has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum. To find them:

items: Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region and the values of $f$ there.
On each piece of the boundary, write $f$ as a function of one variable and find its critical points.
Include the corners (the endpoints of the boundary pieces).
The largest value in the whole list is the absolute maximum; the smallest is the absolute minimum.

blocks.html: Where can the maximum be? If it is at an interior point, $f$ is locally largest there, so $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$: step 1 catches it. If it is on the boundary, it is in particular the largest value of $f$ along that edge, which is a one-variable problem: either a critical point of the edge function or an end of the edge, a corner. Steps 2 and 3 catch those. Nothing else is possible, so comparing the finite list is enough.

blocks.cap: $f = x^2 + y^2 - 2x - 4y$ over the square $[0, 3] \times [0, 3]$. The bottom of the bowl is inside, at $(1, 2)$; the highest point is a corner. The red slice is the edge $x = 3$, where $f$ becomes the one-variable function $y^2 - 4y + 3$.

blocks.title: On a square
blocks.q: Find the absolute extremes of $f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 2x - 4y$ on ${}0 \le x \le 3$, ${}0 \le y \le 3$.

blocks.title: On a triangle
blocks.q: Find the absolute extremes of $f(x, y) = 2x^2 + y^2 - 4x$ on the triangle with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(2, 0)$, $(0, 2)$.
steps: Inside: $f_x = 4x - 4 = 0$ and $f_y = 2y = 0$ give $(1, 0)$, which is on the edge, not inside.
Edge $y = 0$: ${}2x^2 - 4x$, critical at $x = 1$: $f = -2$. Edge $x = 0$: $y^2$, no interior critical point.

blocks.html: Skipping the boundary, or its corners. Setting $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$ only finds interior candidates. In the first example the maximum, ${}3$, is at a corner, where neither partial derivative is zero. Each edge needs its own one-variable search, and every corner must be on the list, because the edge functions are only defined on closed intervals.

blocks.html: Often you cannot go anywhere you like: you must stay on a curve or a surface. Maximize the area of a fence with a fixed length, or find the hottest point on a circular wire. That is constrained optimization: extremes of $f$ subject to $g(x, y) = k$. The key picture uses two facts you know: the gradient is perpendicular to level curves, and a level curve of $f$ that crosses the constraint cannot mark an extreme.

At a maximum or minimum of $f$ on the curve $g(x, y) = k$ (with $ abla g e \mathbf{0}$), the gradients are parallel: $$ abla f = \lambda abla g, \qquad g(x, y) = k.$$ Solve this system for $x$, $y$ and $\lambda$ (the Lagrange multiplier), then evaluate $f$ at every solution and compare.

Move along the constraint curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$. If $f$ has its largest value on the curve at $\mathbf{r}(t_0)$, then $ rac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) = abla f \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$ is ${}0$ at $t_0$: $ abla f$ is perpendicular to the curve. But $ abla g$ is also perpendicular to the curve, because the curve is a level curve of $g$. In the plane, two vectors perpendicular to the same direction are parallel, so $ abla f = \lambda abla g$. In pictures: at the extreme, the level curve of $f$ just touches the constraint curve without crossing it.

steps: $y = 2\lambda x$ and $x = 2\lambda y$. Then $y = 4\lambda^2 y$, so $y = 0$ or $\lambda = \pm\frac{1}{2}$.

blocks.title: Closest point on a plane
blocks.q: Find the point of the plane $x + 2y + 2z = 9$ closest to the origin.
steps: Minimize the squared distance $f = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ with $g = x + 2y + 2z = 9$.
The constraint gives $\frac{\lambda}{2}(1 + 4 + 4) = 9$, so $\frac{\lambda}{2} = 1$: the point $(1, 2, 2)$, at distance ${}3$.

blocks.html: Solving for $\lambda$ and stopping. The multiplier is a helper, not the answer. The system usually has several solutions; each is a candidate, and you must evaluate $f$ at all of them (as in the second example, where two give the maximum and two the minimum). Also watch for lost solutions: dividing an equation by $x$ or $y$ can throw away the case where that variable is ${}0$, so factor instead.

blocks.html: Two constraints in space, $g(x, y, z) = k_1$ and $h(x, y, z) = k_2$, are two surfaces; together they usually cut out a curve, like the ellipse where a plane slices a cylinder. Optimizing on that curve extends Lagrange multipliers with a second multiplier.

At a maximum or minimum of $f$ on the curve where $g = k_1$ and $h = k_2$ (with $
abla g$, $
abla h$ not parallel):
  $$
abla f = \lambda
abla g + \mu
abla h, \qquad g = k_1, \qquad h = k_2.$$
  That is five equations in $x$, $y$, $z$, $\lambda$, $\mu$. Evaluate $f$ at every solution.

Let $\mathbf{T}$ be the tangent direction of the curve at the extreme point. As before, $
abla f \cdot \mathbf{T} = 0$. The curve lies in both surfaces, so $\mathbf{T}$ is perpendicular to $
abla g$ and to $
abla h$. The vectors perpendicular to $\mathbf{T}$ form a plane, and $
abla g$ and $
abla h$ span it (they are not parallel). So $
abla f$, which also lies in that plane, is a combination $\lambda
abla g + \mu
abla h$.

blocks.q: Find the extremes of $f = z$ on the curve $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, $x + y + z = 2$.
steps: Components: ${}0 = 2\lambda x + \mu$, ${}0 = 2\lambda y + \mu$, ${}1 = \mu$. So ${}2\lambda x = 2\lambda y = -1$, which forces $x = y$.
With $x^2 + y^2 = 1$: $x = y = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, and $z = 2 - x - y = 2 \mp \sqrt{2}$.

blocks.title: Closest point of a line
blocks.q: Minimize $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ subject to $x + y + z = 3$ and $x - y = 1$.

blocks.html: Sometimes a constraint can simply be solved for one variable. In the first example, $z = 2 - x - y$ turns the problem into one constraint in the plane. Both routes give the same answer; Lagrange's method is the one that always works, even when solving is messy.

Using only one multiplier. Writing $\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$ and ignoring $h$ finds extremes on the whole surface $g = k_1$, not on the curve. Each constraint brings its own multiplier and its own equation. Count: unknowns $x, y, z, \lambda, \mu$ (five) must match equations (three gradient components plus two constraints).

blocks.html: The gradient points uphill as steeply as possible. To find a low point, you have been setting $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$ and solving, as with critical points. That works for small textbook functions. For a function of a thousand variables, or a million, nobody can solve that system. There is a humbler plan: stand somewhere, feel which way is down, take a step, and repeat.

Gradient descent: choose a starting point $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ and a step size $\eta > 0$ (also called the learning rate). Then repeat $$\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_{k} - \eta\,\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{k}).$$ Each step goes against the gradient, the direction of steepest descent, by an amount proportional to how steep the ground is.

By the linear approximation, $$f(\mathbf{x} - \eta abla f) \approx f(\mathbf{x}) - \eta\, abla f \cdot abla f = f(\mathbf{x}) - \eta\,| abla f|^{2}.$$ When $ abla f e \mathbf{0}$ and $\eta$ is small, that is less than $f(\mathbf{x})$: a small enough step always goes down. And the points stop moving only where $ abla f = \mathbf{0}$, at a critical point.

blocks.title: The step size decides everything
blocks.q: Run gradient descent on $f(x) = x^{2}$ from $x_{0} = 2$ with $\eta = 0.1$, $0.5$, $0.9$ and $1.1$.
steps: $f'(x) = 2x$, so $x_{k+1} = x_{k} - 2\eta x_{k} = (1 - 2\eta)x_{k}$. Every step multiplies by $r = 1 - 2\eta$.
$\eta = 0.5$: $r = 0$. One step lands exactly on the minimum.
$\eta = 0.9$: $r = -0.8$. The points $2, -1.6, 1.28, \ldots$ jump across the minimum each time, but still close in.
$\eta = 1.1$: $r = -1.2$. The points $2, -2.4, 2.88, \ldots$ land farther out every time: the run blows up.
blocks.a: It converges for $0 < \eta < 1$, fastest at $\eta = 0.5$, and blows up for $\eta > 1$.

blocks.name: calc3-descent
blocks.cap: $f(x) = x^{2}$ with $\eta = 0.9$: each step jumps across the bottom. Try $\eta = 0.1$, $0.5$ and $1.1$, then Reset. The red arrow is the next step.

blocks.title: Steps on a bowl
blocks.q: Take two steps on $f(x, y) = x^{2} + 3y^{2}$ from $(2, 1)$ with $\eta = 0.1$.
steps: Each step multiplies $x$ by $1 - 2\eta = 0.8$ and $y$ by $1 - 6\eta = 0.4$: the steep direction shrinks faster.

blocks.html: Those factors also set a speed limit. In the $y$-direction the factor $1 - 6\eta$ has size less than $1$ only when $\eta < \frac{1}{3}$; in the $x$-direction the limit is $\eta < 1$. The steepest direction sets the limit for the whole run. In a long, narrow valley that limit is small, so progress along the gentle floor of the valley is slow, and the path zigzags across it.

blocks.name: calc3-descent
blocks.cap: Drag the ball (or tap the map) to start somewhere new, then press Run. In the long valley, $f = \frac{x^{2}}{2} + 5y^{2}$, a step size near $0.2$ zigzags and anything above $0.2$ blows up. Then switch to Two valleys.

blocks.title: Not always the lowest point
blocks.q: Run gradient descent with a small step size on $f(x) = x^{4} - 4x^{2} + x$, once from $x_{0} = 1$ and once from $x_{0} = -1$.
steps: $f'(x) = 4x^{3} - 8x + 1$, whose zeros are near $x \approx -1.47$, $0.13$ and $1.35$: two valleys with a hill between them.
From $x_{0} = 1$: $f'(1) = -3 < 0$, so the steps go right and settle near $x \approx 1.35$, where $f \approx -2.62$.
From $x_{0} = -1$: $f'(-1) = 5 > 0$, so the steps go left and settle near $x \approx -1.47$, where $f \approx -5.44$.
Both are local minima. Gradient descent stops at the bottom of whichever valley it starts in, and only the second one is the lowest point.
blocks.a: It finds the valley it starts in, which may not hold the lowest point.

blocks.html: Stepping uphill. $\mathbf{x}_{k} + \eta\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{k})$ climbs, because the gradient points uphill. Check: work out $f$ before and after a small step. It should go down.

Thinking a bigger step is always faster. Past the limit set by the steepest direction, each step overshoots by more than it gains and the run blows up. Check: if $f$ goes up after a step, halve $\eta$.

In machine learning, $f$ is a loss: a number that measures how badly a model fits its examples, as a function of the model's weights. Gradient descent, run on millions of weights at once, is how neural networks are trained. Next you will fit a line this way (minimizing loss) and find a network's gradient (backpropagation).

blocks.html: In Probability and Statistics you met the least-squares line, the line with the smallest sum of squared residuals, and used formulas for its slope and intercept. Here you will see where those formulas come from, and a second way to find the same line: the way that scales up to models with millions of parameters.

A model $\hat{y} = mx + b$ has two parameters, $m$ and $b$. Its loss on the data $(x_{1}, y_{1}), \ldots, (x_{n}, y_{n})$ is the mean squared error $$L(m, b) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_{i} - (mx_{i} + b)\right)^{2}.$$ Fitting the model means minimizing $L$: either solve $\nabla L = \mathbf{0}$ exactly, or run gradient descent on $L$.

The data are fixed numbers; the variables are $m$ and $b$. The inside $y_{i} - mx_{i} - b$ has derivative $-x_{i}$ with respect to $m$ and $-1$ with respect to $b$, so by the chain rule $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial m} = -\frac{2}{n}\sum x_{i}\left(y_{i} - mx_{i} - b\right), \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = -\frac{2}{n}\sum \left(y_{i} - mx_{i} - b\right).$$ Setting both to $0$ gives the normal equations $$m\sum x_{i}^{2} + b\sum x_{i} = \sum x_{i}y_{i}, \qquad m\sum x_{i} + nb = \sum y_{i}.$$ $L$ is a quadratic bowl: its second-derivative test gives $D = \frac{4}{n^{2}}\left(n\sum x_{i}^{2} - \left(\sum x_{i}\right)^{2}\right) > 0$ whenever the $x_{i}$ are not all equal. So its one critical point is the minimum, the least-squares line.

blocks.name: calc3-fitline
blocks.cap: Left: the data, the line and its squared residuals. Right: the loss over the $(m, b)$-plane. Each step of gradient descent moves the red dot downhill, and the line on the left follows. Press Show the exact answer to compare.

blocks.title: The exact answer
blocks.q: Find the line that minimizes $L$ for the data $(0, 1)$, $(1, 3)$, $(2, 4)$, $(3, 4)$, $(4, 6)$.
steps: Double the second, $20m + 10b = 36$, and subtract: $10m = 11$, so $m = 1.1$. Then $5b = 18 - 11$, so $b = 1.4$.

blocks.title: One step of gradient descent
blocks.q: Same data. Start at $(m, b) = (0, 0)$ and take one gradient descent step with $\eta = 0.05$.
steps: At $(0, 0)$ every prediction is $0$, so the residuals are the $y_{i}$ themselves.
$\frac{\partial L}{\partial m} = -\frac{2}{5}\sum x_{i}y_{i} = -\frac{2}{5} \cdot 47 = -18.8$ and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = -\frac{2}{5}\sum y_{i} = -\frac{2}{5} \cdot 18 = -7.2$.
The loss falls from $L(0, 0) = 15.6$ to $L(0.94, 0.36) \approx 2.12$. More steps creep toward $(1.1, 1.4)$.

blocks.title: A line through the origin
steps: With one parameter the loss is a parabola: $$L(m) = \frac{1}{3}\left[(3 - m)^{2} + (2 - 2m)^{2} + (7 - 3m)^{2}\right] = \frac{1}{3}\left(14m^{2} - 56m + 62\right).$$
$L'(m) = \frac{1}{3}(28m - 56) = 0$ gives $m = 2$, the vertex of the parabola.

blocks.html: In the picture the loss map is a long, tilted valley, because $\sum x_{i}^{2} = 30$ is much bigger than $n = 5$. As in gradient descent on a long valley, a step size above about $0.15$ makes the path blow up, and a small one crawls along the valley floor. For a straight line the exact answer is easy, so why bother with steps? Because most models have no formula. A neural network's loss is also a mean of squared errors, but of a bent-line function of its weights, and there gradient descent, with derivatives from backpropagation, is the tool that works.

Differentiating with respect to $x$. In $L(m, b)$ the $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ are numbers you were given; they never change. The variables are the parameters. Check: your $\frac{\partial L}{\partial m}$ should contain data values, $m$ and $b$, and no plain $x$.

Dropping the minus sign. The inside $y_{i} - mx_{i} - b$ has derivative $-x_{i}$ with respect to $m$, so $\frac{\partial L}{\partial m}$ starts with $-\frac{2}{n}$. Without that sign a gradient step climbs. Check: with positive data, a step from $(0, 0)$ should raise both $m$ and $b$.
This is the same line as ordinary least squares in the Econometrics course, and the normal equations are the matrix equation of least squares in linear algebra.

blocks.html: To train a network by gradient descent, you need the derivative of its loss with respect to every weight. Here is the smallest network that shows how, with one input $x$, one hidden ramp unit and one output: $$z = wx + b, \qquad h = \operatorname{ReLU}(z), \qquad \hat{y} = vh + c, \qquad L = (\hat{y} - y)^{2},$$ for one data point $(x, y)$. The loss depends on the weights $w$, $b$, $v$ and $c$ through a chain of simple steps, so the tool is the chain rule.

Backpropagation: run the network forward and keep $z$, $h$, $\hat{y}$ and $L$. Then go backward, multiplying by one local derivative per step: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}} = 2(\hat{y} - y), \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial h} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}}\,v, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial h}\,\operatorname{ReLU}'(z),$$ where $\operatorname{ReLU}'(z)$ is $1$ when the switch is on ($z > 0$) and $0$ when it is off. Each weight's derivative is the derivative at its node times what the weight multiplies: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial v} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}}\,h, \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}}, \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z}\,x, \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z}.$$

Each formula is the chain rule along the one path from $L$ down to that weight, as in a tree diagram: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial h} \cdot \frac{\partial h}{\partial z} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial w}.$$ Working backward, the shared front part of these products, such as $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z}$, is computed once and reused for $w$ and $b$. In a network with millions of weights that reuse is the whole point: one backward pass costs about as much as a couple of forward passes, instead of one forward pass per weight.

blocks.name: calc3-backprop
blocks.cap: Press Next step to run forward, then backward. Orange numbers are derivatives of the loss. After the last step, the table checks each one with a nudge, and Take a gradient step uses them to lower the loss.

blocks.title: All four derivatives
blocks.q: With $w = 1$, $b = -1$, $v = 2$, $c = 0.5$ and the data point $(x, y) = (2, 3)$, find $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$, $\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}$, $\frac{\partial L}{\partial v}$ and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial c}$.
steps: Start at the loss: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}} = 2(2.5 - 3) = -1$. So $\frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = -1$ and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial v} = -1 \cdot h = -1$.
Into the hidden unit: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial h} = -1 \cdot v = -2$. The switch is on ($z = 1 > 0$), so $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = -2$.
Into the first layer: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = -2 \cdot x = -4$ and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = -2$.
All four are negative: the prediction $2.5$ is too low, and raising any weight a little would raise it.
blocks.a: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = -4$, $\frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = -2$, $\frac{\partial L}{\partial v} = -1$, $\frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = -1$

blocks.title: Check with a nudge
blocks.q: Check $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = -4$ numerically.
steps: $\frac{0.246016 - 0.254016}{0.002} = -4$. ✓ This check costs two forward passes for each weight; backpropagation found all four derivatives in one backward pass.

blocks.title: When the switch is off
blocks.q: Same weights, but the data point is $(x, y) = (-1, 1)$.
steps: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}} = -1$, so $\frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = -1$, but $\frac{\partial L}{\partial v} = -1 \cdot 0 = 0$.
The switch is off: $\operatorname{ReLU}'(-2) = 0$, so $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = 0$ and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = 0$.
Small changes to $w$ and $b$ leave $z$ negative and the output unchanged, so this example cannot teach them anything. Only $c$ learns from it.

blocks.html: With more units the same rules run on vectors. For a layer $\mathbf{h} = \operatorname{ReLU}(W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b})$ the backward step is $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{h}} \odot \operatorname{ReLU}'(\mathbf{z}), \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}}\,\mathbf{x}^{T}, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = W^{T}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}},$$ where $\odot$ multiplies entry by entry. The last formula hands the signal to the layer before, which repeats the same steps. With many data points, average the gradients from each one. The network that trains itself in Neural Network Layers works exactly this way.

Forgetting the switch. On the way back, ReLU multiplies by $1$ if its unit was on and by $0$ if it was off. Skipping it gives a nonzero $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$ for an off unit, as if a weight could change an output it does not reach. Check: if $z < 0$, the derivatives for $w$ and $b$ must be $0$.

Multiplying by the wrong thing. $\frac{\partial z}{\partial w} = x$: the derivative with respect to a weight uses the input that the weight multiplies, not the weight itself. Check with a nudge: change the weight by $0.001$ and see how much $L$ changes.
At exactly $z = 0$ the ramp has a corner and no derivative. Software simply uses $0$ (or $1$) there, and it rarely matters; the practice problems avoid that point.

blocks.html: In Calculus 1 the definite integral was built from thin rectangles under a curve. A surface $z = f(x, y)$ over a rectangle $R$ in the plane encloses a solid, and its volume is built the same way from thin boxes.

Divide $R$ into small rectangles of area $\Delta A$, pick a sample point $(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)$ in each, and add up box volumes: $$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA = \lim_{m, n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} f(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)\,\Delta A.$$ If $f \ge 0$ this is the volume under the surface; parts below the $xy$-plane count as negative. The average value of $f$ on $R$ is $\frac{1}{\text{area}(R)}\iint_R f\,dA$.

Over one small rectangle the surface is nearly flat, so the solid above it is nearly a box with base $\Delta A$ and height $f$ at the sample point. Each box is slightly too tall or too short, but for a continuous $f$ the surface varies less and less across a smaller rectangle, so the total error goes to ${}0$ as the grid gets finer. The sums settle on one number, the double integral. Sums split and constants factor out, so the integral is linear: $$\iint (af + bg)\,dA = a\iint f\,dA + b\iint g\,dA.$$

blocks.name: calc3-boxes
blocks.cap: Boxes under $z = 4 - \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{y^2}{4}$ over $[0, 2] \times [0, 2]$. Raise $n$ and the sum of the box volumes closes in on the integral; switch the sample point to see a cruder estimate.

blocks.title: The midpoint rule
blocks.q: Estimate $\iint_R (x + 2y)\,dA$ on $R = [0, 2] \times [0, 2]$ with a ${}2 \times 2$ grid and midpoints.
steps: Estimate $= 12 \cdot 1 = 12$. (For a function like this, whose graph is a plane, the midpoint rule is exact.)

blocks.title: Average value
blocks.q: Find the average value of $f(x, y) = xy$ on $R = [0, 2] \times [0, 4]$.
steps: $$\iint_R xy\,dA = \left(\int_0^2 x\,dx\right)\left(\int_0^4 y\,dy\right) = 2 \cdot 8 = 16$$ (the integral of a product $g(x)h(y)$ over a rectangle splits).
A flat box of height ${}2$ over $R$ holds the same volume as the region under the surface.

blocks.title: Linearity
blocks.q: If $\iint_R f\,dA = 5$ and $\iint_R g\,dA = -2$ on a rectangle of area ${}3$, find $\iint_R (3f - 2g + 1)\,dA$.

blocks.html: Forgetting $\Delta A$ in a Riemann sum. Adding the heights alone gives a number that changes when you refine the grid. Each term is a volume: height times base area. Check: doubling $m$ and $n$ should give a similar estimate, not one four times as big. Also remember that a double integral is a signed volume: if $f$ dips below zero, that part subtracts.

blocks.html: Riemann sums define a double integral, but nobody computes one that way. Instead, integrate one variable at a time, the way you found volumes by slicing in Calculus 2.

Fubini's theorem: for continuous $f$ on $R = [a, b] \times [c, d]$, $$\iint_R f\,dA = \int_a^b \left(\int_c^d f(x, y)\,dy\right) dx = \int_c^d \left(\int_a^b f(x, y)\,dx\right) dy.$$ Work from the inside out; in the inner integral, the outer variable is a constant.

Slice the solid with a plane $x = c$ (a constant). The slice is a region under the curve $z = f(x, y)$, $c \le y \le d$, with area $A(x) = \int_c^d f(x, y)\,dy$. A slab of thickness $\Delta x$ has volume about $A(x)\,\Delta x$, and adding slabs gives $\int_a^b A(x)\,dx$. Slicing with planes $y = c$ instead gives the other order. Both compute the same volume, which is why the order does not change the answer.

blocks.name: surface
blocks.cap: The red slice at $x = c$ has area $A(c) = \int_0^2 f(c, y)\,dy$, the inner integral. Slide it from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$: adding up those areas gives the volume.

blocks.html:
When the integrand is a product $g(x)h(y)$ over a rectangle, the iterated integral splits into two single integrals:
  $$\int_a^b \int_c^d g(x)h(y)\,dy\,dx = \left(\int_a^b g(x)\,dx\right)\left(\int_c^d h(y)\,dy\right),$$
  because in the inner integral $g(x)$ is a constant that can come outside. For example, $\int_0^1 \int_0^\pi x\sin y\,dy\,dx = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 = 1$. Fubini's theorem also allows switching the order, which matters when one order leads to an antiderivative you cannot find; the third example below shows this.

blocks.title: Inside out
blocks.q: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^2\int_1^3 x^2y\,dy\,dx$.
steps: Inner, in $y$ ($x$ is a constant): $\int_1^3 x^2y\,dy = x^2\left[\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_1^3 = x^2 \cdot 4 = 4x^2$.

blocks.title: The other order
blocks.q: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^3\int_0^2 x^2y\,dx\,dy$.
steps: Outer: $\int_1^3 \frac{8}{3}y\,dy = \frac{8}{3} \cdot 4 = \frac{32}{3}$, the same, as Fubini promises.

blocks.title: Choosing the easy order
blocks.q: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\int_0^2 xe^{xy}\,dy\,dx$.
steps: Inner in $y$: $\int_0^2 xe^{xy}\,dy = \left[e^{xy}\right]_{y=0}^{y=2} = e^{2x} - 1$ (the $x$ in front is exactly the inner derivative).
Integrating $x$ first would need integration by parts: both orders are correct, but one is much easier.

blocks.html: Mismatching limits and differentials. In $\int_a^b\int_c^d f\,dy\,dx$, the inner limits $c$ to $d$ belong to $y$ (the inner differential $dy$) and the outer limits to $x$. Writing $dx\,dy$ while keeping the $x$-limits inside integrates over a different rectangle. Read from the inside out: innermost integral sign, innermost differential.

blocks.html: Most regions are not rectangles. In area between curves you sliced a region vertically, with each slice running from a lower curve to an upper curve. Do the same for a double integral, and let the inner limits be those curves.

Type I (vertical slices): $D = \{a \le x \le b,\ g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)\}$ gives $$\displaystyle\iint_D f\,dA = \int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx.$$
Type II (horizontal slices): $D = \{c \le y \le d,\ h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)\}$ gives $\displaystyle\int_c^d\int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f\,dx\,dy$.
Inner limits may depend on the outer variable; outer limits are always constants. The area of $D$ is $\iint_D 1\,dA$.

Fix $x$ and look at the vertical line through the region: it enters at the lower boundary $y = g_1(x)$ and leaves at the upper boundary $y = g_2(x)$. The inner integral adds $f$ along that slice only, so it naturally depends on $x$. The outer integral then sweeps the slices across, from the leftmost to the rightmost $x$ in the region; those are fixed numbers, because they describe the whole region, not one slice. After integrating, no variable may be left, and that happens only if the outer limits are constants.

blocks.name: calc3-region
blocks.cap: The region between $y = x^2$ and $y = x$. Move the slice: its ends always sit on the two curves. Switch to horizontal slices to describe the same region with $x$ inside.

blocks.title: Between two curves
blocks.q: Evaluate $\iint_D (x + y)\,dA$ where $D$ is the region between $y = x^2$ and $y = x$.
steps: The curves meet at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, and $x \ge x^2$ there: ${}0 \le x \le 1$, $x^2 \le y \le x$.

blocks.title: An area
blocks.q: Find the area between $y = x^2$ and $y = 2x$.
steps: They meet at $x = 0$ and $x = 2$; the line is on top.

blocks.title: Horizontal slices are easier
blocks.q: Find the area of the region bounded by $x = y^2$ and $x = y + 2$.
steps: Vertical slices would need two pieces, but horizontally the region runs from the parabola $x = y^2$ (left) to the line $x = y + 2$ (right).

blocks.html: Putting variables in the outer limits. An answer like $\int_{x^2}^{x}\int_0^1 \ldots\,dy\,dx$ is upside down: after the inner integral you would integrate in $x$ between limits that contain $x$, which makes no sense. The outer integral describes the whole region with numbers; the inner one describes a single slice with curves. Check: your final answer must be a number.

blocks.html: Sometimes the inner integral is impossible as written: $\int e^{y^2}\,dy$ and $\int \sin(x^2)\,dx$ have no elementary antiderivative. But the region of integration can be sliced the other way. If you can describe a general region with vertical slices, you can usually describe it with horizontal ones, and the integral may become easy.

To reverse the order: draw the region from the given limits, then describe the same region with slices in the other direction. The new outer limits are the full range of the new outer variable; the new inner limits are the boundary curves solved for the inner variable.

The value of a double integral depends only on the function and the region, not on how you slice it: both orders add up $f\,dA$ over exactly the same points. So any correct description of the region gives the same number. Swapping the limits mechanically does not describe the same region, which is why the picture is essential.

blocks.name: calc3-region
blocks.cap: The triangle ${}0 \le x \le 1$, $x \le y \le 1$. Vertical slices run from $y = x$ up to $y = 1$; switch to horizontal slices and they run from $x = 0$ to $x = y$, for ${}0 \le y \le 1$.

blocks.title: An impossible inner integral
blocks.q: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\int_x^1 e^{y^2}\,dy\,dx$.
steps: The region: ${}0 \le x \le 1$, $x \le y \le 1$, the triangle with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, 1)$.
$\int_0^1\int_0^y e^{y^2}\,dx\,dy = \int_0^1 ye^{y^2}\,dy$: the inner integral produced the factor $y$.

blocks.title: Just the limits
blocks.q: Reverse the order in $\displaystyle\int_0^4\int_{\sqrt{y}}^{2} f(x, y)\,dx\,dy$.
steps: Region: ${}0 \le y \le 4$, and $x$ from the curve $x = \sqrt{y}$ (that is, $y = x^2$) to the line $x = 2$.
It is the region under the parabola $y = x^2$ for ${}0 \le x \le 2$.

blocks.title: A root
blocks.q: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\int_{\sqrt{y}}^1 \sqrt{x^3 + 1}\,dx\,dy$.

blocks.html: Swapping the limits without redrawing the region. Turning $\int_0^1\int_x^1 \ldots\,dy\,dx$ into $\int_x^1\int_0^1 \ldots\,dx\,dy$ leaves an $x$ in the outer limits; turning it into $\int_0^1\int_x^1 \ldots\,dx\,dy$ describes a different region. Sketch first, read the extreme values of the new outer variable off the picture, then solve each boundary curve for the new inner variable. Check: both orders give the same area when you integrate ${}1$.
